# What are these hoses for on a Honda Jazz?

When diagnosing fluid leaks in older vehicles, visual inspection of the undertray often reveals the source before the engine bay does. In your specific case involving a 2007 Honda Jazz 1.4 DSi CVT, the clear, cool-to-touch fluid that appears only when the air conditioning is active is almost certainly refrigerant or condensate water. The two hoses you identified are integral to the vehicle's thermal management and humidity control systems, specifically the Air Conditioning (A/C) and Automatic Transmission Cooling loops.

### The Left Hose: Condensate Drainage

The primary suspect for the dripping fluid on your floor mats is the left hose connected to the evaporator case. Inside the cabin, the A/C evaporator acts as a heat exchanger, removing thermal energy from the air while simultaneously stripping moisture. As warm, humid air passes over the cold evaporator fins, water vapor condenses into liquid.

This accumulated condensate must be removed to prevent pooling within the HVAC plenum or dripping directly onto the passenger footwell. The hose you located connects the drain port on the bottom of the evaporator assembly to a designated drainage pointâusually routed through the firewall or into the subframe near the strut tower. This path ensures gravity assists the drainage process, preventing backflow.

If this line is restricted by debris (common in high-mileage vehicles) or if the hose itself has degraded and developed micro-fractures, you will observe a steady leak. The fact that the drips are cool to the touch confirms the fluid is not oil from the engine or transmission, as those components would be hot when the engine is at operating temperature.

### The Right Hose: Transmission Cooler Lines

The second hose visible in your photos likely serves the automatic transmission cooler lines. In front-wheel-drive vehicles like the Honda Jazz, the transmission relies on a dedicated coolant loop to regulate oil temperature. These lines run from the transmission pan (or the internal cooler housing) to the radiator or an auxiliary cooler located in the front bumper area.

While these are hydraulic lines rather than simple drainage hoses, they can leak if the O-rings at the banjo bolts or hose fittings degrade. However, transmission fluid is typically reddish-orange and has a distinct petroleum odor, unlike the clear, odourless water you described. If this line were leaking, you would likely see fluid pooling near the front axle housing or dripping from the undercarriage regardless of A/C usage.

### Corrective Action and Long-Term Stability

Since the leak is active and located at the base of the vehicle, corrective action is required to prevent corrosion to the underbody and potential electrical shorts. The immediate trade-off here involves cost versus longevity. Replacing a short section of rubber hose with new silicone tubing or OEM replacements is a standard repair. However, if the hose has been vibrating against the metal subframe for 17 years (from 2007 to present), the surrounding area may have developed micro-abrasions or rust that could compromise the new installation.

Before purchasing parts, inspect the drain pan located directly beneath the evaporator. If the pan is cracked, replacing the hose alone will not solve the problem; the fluid will simply bypass the clog and leak through the pan. You can verify this by gently blowing compressed air into the hose (with the A/C off) to clear minor obstructions, though a complete flush might be necessary if the restriction is severe.

It is also worth noting that the evaporator case itself can develop hairline cracks over time due to thermal cycling. If replacing the hoses yields no improvement after a few days of operation under load, the evaporator assembly may require replacement. This is a more invasive job requiring the removal of the dashboard, but it is a known wear item for high-mileage DSi models.

For detailed diagrams regarding the specific routing of these lines on your chassis code, you might find utility in technical service bulletins or specialized repair guides that often reference platforms like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) for structured vehicle data, though standard Honda service manuals remain the definitive source for torque specs and part numbers.
